items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.title: [Fast Company] Why the government wants self-driving cars to glow cyan
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Robotaxis and other self-driving cars could soon get their own distinct cyan-colored lights to show when they’re being driven by a robot.

The bright blue-green color would be standardized for automated driving system marker lamps under a new proposal for federal AV requirements. These and other standards were announced Oct. 23 by the Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

Cyan lights would let motorists and law enforcement know when an automated system is operating a vehicle, NHTSA said. The color was chosen because it’s not used for anything else and has industry backing.

SAE International, an aerospace and automotive professional association, recommends cyan for AVs because it says a unique color would have a clear meaning, unlike standard light colors like amber, red, or white. The group says it selected blue-green after asking manufacturers, suppliers, research organizations, and experts about several potential light color options, and NHTSA says the specifications for the cyan they’d set are different enough from the blue lights some states reserve for law enforcement or towing.

NHTSA’s proposal is now open to a 30-day public comment period, and the agency’s administrator Jonathan Morrison said in a statement it establishes “clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps” and paves the way for “safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”

Mercedes-Benz introduced turquoise lights in 2023 on its EQS sedan and S-class permitted that year in California and Nevada to indicate when the vehicles were set to the automaker’s “Drive Pilot” mode. The automaker said it worked with engineers, compliance managers, data protection officers, and ethics experts on selecting the color, adding that tests showed teal was clearly distinguishable from traffic and emergency lighting.

Living in the future

Cyan also works for AVs for the simple reason that it looks futuristic. It’s a color found in sci-fi films, like Disney’s 2010 Tron: Legacy. When you see turquoise lights on the exterior mirrors and front and rear lights of a Mercedes, or cyan lights on a funny-looking robotaxi, it instantly communicates “technology.” Motorists in cities where AVs are already being road tested will likely understand the color represents a vehicle that’s either autonomous, electric, or otherwise high tech.

As far as creating a visual shorthand goes, cyan is actually a pretty intuitive color to do it with. Mercedes suggests educational measures before and during market launch could inform the public about what the color stands for, but even without it, the color does its job to communicate automation thanks to its association with science fiction and the future.

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] Malicious vendor script targeted Polymarket sessions to drain crypto portfolios
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Malicious JavaScript delivered through a website-monitoring integration sought to take over logged-in Polymarket traders’ sessions and redirect their assets, cybersecurity researchers said. Polymarket confirmed that a third-party provider was compromised and referred the incident to law enforcement, but did not publicly name the vendor. Researchers said the script read account data from browser storage, searched Polymarket’s application for its live trading client and signer, then attempted transactions using that existing access. Depending on the account type, it tried either to transfer position tokens or to sell positions and move the proceeds. Hudson Rock, which analyzed the sample, did not execute it, so its findings describe intended behavior rather than establish that every attempted transfer succeeded. Polymarket’s production build metadata showed that the DebugBear monitoring script was removed at 1:59 p.m. ET on Oct. 29, shortly before the company announced the incident, BleepingComputer reported. DebugBear separately told customers using its Real User Monitoring product to remove the embedded code and said it had brought in incident-response specialists.

items.title: [space.com] Soviet Union sent Laika into orbit aboard Sputnik 2 with no return plan
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2 with Laika aboard on Nov. 3, 1957, making the Moscow stray the first animal to orbit Earth. The spacecraft had no system to bring her back, and Laika died within hours as the capsule overheated, according to later accounts. The flight came less than a month after Sputnik 1 and aimed to test how a living organism responded to launch and weightlessness. Sensors transmitted Laika’s vital signs to Earth, but Soviet officials initially said she had survived for days. Details of her early death from overheating became public decades later. Sputnik 2 remained in orbit until it burned up on re-entry on April 14, 1958.

The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.title: [cloud.google.com] Google bans Chinese partner after backdoor infects 1.3 million Android boxes
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Google and security partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, which had enrolled more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes. Google says it has high confidence that Shenzhen-based manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co. deliberately embedded the backdoor in device firmware and sold criminal groups access to infected hardware. The criminal groups used the devices to commit advertising fraud, route other people’s internet traffic through household connections and install additional malware. Google also reported that operators captured screens, collected account information and system logs, and issued commands remotely. The same malware appeared on telehealth equipment, karaoke machines and digital signs. Google’s takedown targeted XCPE control servers and domains used by more than a dozen related malware families. Google estimates the takedown could also cut criminal access to at least 10 million other devices compromised through separate routes. Videostrong evaded Google’s device checks by loading malicious code after a device’s first boot, Google said. Google has banned Videostrong and its future affiliates from making certified Android devices or supplying software to certified manufacturers, and says it changed its review process. The backdoor remains in affected devices and can reinstall after a reboot. Synthient, a security firm involved in the investigation, recommends disconnecting and replacing affected boxes.
